title: Serving Runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarks, runbooks
author: Daniel Kim
content:
Overview
--------
This document consolidates the serving runtime reference for Redwood Inference: architecture, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling/playbook steps, benchmarking suite guidance, release-note checklist for runtime changes, known issues with mitigations, and operational runbooks. It is intended for Runtime Engineers, Applied ML, SRE, and Platform teams who maintain latency, throughput, and cost SLOs for hosted and dedicated deployments.

Scope
-----
- System components covered: request routing, scheduling layer, worker runtime, KV/prefix cache, model compilation, kernel selection, telemetry and observability.
- Operational content: profiling procedures, benchmark recipes and CI integration, incident runbooks for performance regressions and capacity issues.
- Not covered: private deployment networking details (see eng-private-deployments reference pages).

1) Runtime architecture (high level)
----------------------------------
Summary: The runtime is a distributed, GPU-optimized inference stack with a thin control plane and horizontally scalable worker pools. Key design goals are predictable p99 latency, high amortized token throughput, and graceful degradation when capacity is constrained.

Components:
- Request Router: accepts REST/SDK requests, performs customer policy routing (latency-tier, cost-tier, region), authenticates and rate-limits. Tags requests with route metadata and preferred kernel profiles.
- Scheduler (control plane): maintains worker pool state, implements batching, preemption, and placement decisions. Accepts scheduling constraints (latency SLO, priority) and produces scheduling decisions (batching windows, assignment to worker shards).
- Worker Runtime (agents on GPU nodes): handles token generation loops, KV cache management, kernel invocation, and model-variant fallback. Exposes health/tracing endpoints.
- KV / Prefix Cache: cross-request and cross-tenant prefix caching layer used for cold-start amortization and repeated prefix hits. Integrated with the scheduler to select cached vs fresh execution.
- Compiler & Kernel Selection: offline and JIT compilation stages produce tuned kernels (FP16/INT8/quantized variants). Runtime selects kernels based on model config, seq length, and device characteristics.
- Observability & Telemetry: per-request traces, token-level cost/latency breakdowns, per-model SLI aggregation.

CRITICAL SLOs and thresholds (examples)
- P50 token latency: <= 2ms (on S-class routing for codegen-7b-like models)
- P95 request latency: <= 120ms for short text generation (<=64 tokens)
- Throughput target per GPU (amortized): 12k tokens/s for baseline 8K context 7b model (depends on kernel profile)
- Error budget: 99.95% availability per production shard per month

Ownership
- Runtime architecture: runtime-platform-team@redwood.internal
- Kernel compilation and perf: compiler-team@redwood.internal
- Observability and SLOs: eng-platform-observability@redwood.internal

2) Kernel scheduling strategies
--------------------------------
Goal: Maximize overall throughput while meeting latency SLOs for priority classes. Key tradeoffs are batching window (throughput) vs latency tail.

Scheduling primitives:
- Batching window (micro-scheduling): worker maintains a short time window (e.g., 1.5ms) to assemble dynamic batches. Window is adaptive based on current p95 and backlog.
- Priority preemption: real-time (tier-1) requests can preempt queued throughput batches. Preempted batches either execute immediately on a spare worker or are downgraded to lower-priority slot.
- Affinity-aware placement: colocate hot-model variants and recent KV cache owners to increase cache hit rates and reduce memory thrash.
- Shard sizing and autoscale signals: scheduler uses recent throughput and p95 targets to size worker shards; autoscale triggers based on sustained 5-minute exceed of target utilization > 75%.

Scheduling algorithms we use:
- Latency-aware hybrid scheduler (default): uses a latency budget per route; when route latency budget is tight, scheduler reduces batching window and prioritizes single-request dispatch. Otherwise it increases batching aggressiveness.
- Cost-oriented batcher: for background/low-priority workloads (embeddings, bulk inference) we switch to larger windows and prefer high-amortization placement.
- Greedy small-batch fallback: if a large batch would exceed memory limits, break into small greedily-packed batches sorted by sequence length to minimize padding overhead.

Config knobs (example table)
- batching.window_ms: 1.5 | 5 | 15 (adaptive)
- batching.max_batch_tokens: 65536
- scheduling.preempt_enabled: true | false
- scheduling.priority_threshold_ms: 50 (requests with SLO budget < threshold become high priority)
- placement.affinity_decay_minutes: 30

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
-------------------------------------
When to profile:
- New model onboarding to determine kernel profile and memory footprint.
- Notable p95/p99 regressions in production after a change.
- GPU OOMs, kernel launch failures, or unexplained throughput drop.

Tools and data sources:
- Tracing: distributed traces (Jaeger), per-request flame graphs exported from worker.
- GPU metrics: nvidia-smi, DCGM, Nsight Systems, CUPTI traces, and Prometheus exporter metrics.
- Microbenchmarks: per-kernel latency logs produced by the kernel harness.
- System counters: CPU steal, host network IO, PCIe transfer times.

Profiling procedure (recommended):
1. Reproduce with a representative load: use benchmark harness with identical model config, sequence lengths, and route tags.
2. Capture distributed trace for 5k requests at target QPS, include per-token timing.
3. Collect GPU-side traces (Nsight Systems) for a 30-60s window that covers the regression and baseline.
4. Correlate: align trace timestamps across host and device, map slow spans to kernel names and memory stages (KV load, kernel exec, memcpy).
5. Isolate cause: common findings are increased memcpy (pinning issue), suboptimal kernel selection (fallback to generic kernel), or padding-induced token waste.
6. Mitigate: tune batching.window_ms, adjust affinity to colocate hot prefixes, pin NUMA/CPU cores for host-to-device memcpy, or roll forward a kernel patch.
7. Validate: re-run the microbench and full-run traces; confirm p95/p99 back within SLO and no regression in throughput.

Quick checklist for in-out profiling:
- Baseline metrics captured (p50/p95/p99 token/request latency, GPU utilization, achieved tokens/s).
- Kernel-level latencies and memory copies.
- Host-level metrics (CPU, network, disk) for cross-correlation.

4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration
--------------------------------------
Purpose: provide repeatable, versioned performance baselines for (a) model variants (FP16 vs INT8), (b) kernel changes, and (c) infra upgrades.

Benchmark types:
- Microbenchmarks: single-GPU, isolated model kernel runs across sequence lengths and batch sizes to produce kernel latency tables.
- End-to-end synthetic workloads: driver that simulates route traffic shapes (short-chat, long-generation, embeddings heavy) and measures per-request SLIs.
- Production-replay: capture anonymized request shapes and replay on staging to measure realistic tails.

Metrics collected:
- Kernel latencies (per op), memcpy times, p50/p95/p99 token latency, tokens/s, GPU SM/utilization, power and energy per token.

CI integration:
- PR gating: Kernel/Runtime PRs must include microbenchmark comparisons; any change worsening p95 by > 5% triggers mandatory rollback or reviewer approval.
- Nightly runs: end-to-end benchmarks run nightly on representative hardware (testbed labels: s-class-gpu, m-class-gpu) and publish trend graphs.
- Canary rollouts: new kernel artifacts deployed to 5% traffic with doubled tracing level for 24-48 hours.

Baseline artifacts and storage:
- Baseline JSONs stored in artifact store with keys: model-id|kernel-profile|date. Each artifact includes inputs used and environment provenance.

5) Release notes and change checklist for runtime/kernel updates
---------------------------------------------------------------
Each release MUST include the following sections in the release notes:
- Summary of change and motivation
- Affected models and routes
- Performance impact analysis vs baseline (p50/p95/p99, tokens/s)
- Memory and OOM risk assessment
- Rollout plan (canary percentage, monitoring flags, rollback criteria)
- Owners and rollback contacts

Pre-release checklist:
1. Microbenchmark and end-to-end benchmarks run and compared.
2. Canary plan configured (5%, 25%, 100%).
3. Monitoring dashboards and alerts included in PR.
4. Runbooks updated for new failure modes.
5. Reviewers: compiler and runtime leads sign off.

6) Known issues and mitigations (living list)
--------------------------------------------
- Intermittent kernel fallback on 80xx GPUs: observed when JIT cache warmup races with multi-tenant compilation. Mitigation: set compilation.fallback_threshold=3 and enable serialized JIT for warmup canary shards.
- Elevated memcpy times with Docker default runtime: pinned across NUMA boundary on some instance types. Mitigation: set container config to use host-numa affinity right after deploy and bump memcpy buffer pool.
- OOM at large sequence lengths (>=32k): observed with model variants compiled with max_seq lower than runtime input. Mitigation: runtime rejects requests > compiled_max_seq with clear 4xx message and routes to fallback trimmed-variant or informs caller.
- p99 regressions after autoscaler events: autoscale leads to cold cache; mitigation: slower ramp-up with staged pre-warm jobs and temporary routing to stable shards during scale events.

If you discover a new known issue please add an entry with: symptoms, reproduction, root-cause hypothesis, mitigation, and owner.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)
-------------------------------------------
A) High p95/p99 latency (production)
1. Triage: check global SLO dashboard and identify affected routes and regions.
2. Run quick perf queries: recent traces, top kernel latencies, recent deploys.
3. If kernel-level increased latencies -> trigger kernel rollback canary.
4. If backlog spike due to traffic surge -> temporarily reduce batching.window_ms for affected routes and scale up shards.
5. If GPUs show OOMs or high PCIe stalls -> drain affected nodes and escalate to infra (eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity).
6. Post-incident: attach trace samples and timeline to incident and update this doc with root cause.

B) GPU OOMs on a shard
1. Identify the offending model variant and request sizes.
2. Temporarily set scheduling.disable_large_batches=true for the shard.
3. Evacuate and reprovision worker with larger memory SKU if sustained.
4. Patch compiler config to limit per-batch allocs and add early rejects for oversized requests.

C) Throughput drop (tokens/s) with normal latency
1. Verify that batching windows and affinity have not changed and that batching.max_batch_tokens wasn't reduced by config.
2. Check PCIe and memcpy times; increased memcpy suggests a host-to-device bottleneck.
3. If host network or disk contention detected, move load or postpone heavy background jobs.
4. If due to scheduling bug, flip scheduling.feature_flag to previous stable value and trigger canary rollback.

8) Team wiki and knowledge resources
------------------------------------
- Primary wiki index: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime (this space)
- Kernel perf dashboard: links stored in eng-platform dashboards (search: "kernel-latency-trends")
- Benchmarking repo: git@internal:redwood/runtime-benchmarks.git (contains harness, datasets, and baseline artifacts)
- Profiling guide notebook: s3://redwood-internal/profiling-notebooks/ (read-only)
- On-call rotation and escalation: see oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process for paging and escalation policy.

Appendix A - common commands and snippets
-----------------------------------------
- Run microbenchmark (example):
  ./bench/harness --model-id codegen-7b --profile fp16 --seq-len=512 --qps=200 --duration=60 --out=baseline.json

- Collect Nsight trace on a worker (short):
  sudo nsys profile --output=nsys_profile --trace-to-console=false --duration=60 --capture-range=cuda

- Extract top kernel latencies from kernel logs:
  jq '.kernels | sort_by(.latency_ms) | reverse | .[0:20]' kernel_latency.json

Appendix B - example config snippet (YAML)
-----------------------------------------
- runtime.config:
  batching:
    window_ms: 5
    max_batch_tokens: 65536
  scheduling:
    preempt_enabled: true
    priority_threshold_ms: 50
  placement:
    affinity_decay_minutes: 30
